results.title: This Tiny USB Device Turns Your Phone Into a Keyboard, Mouse, and SSH Terminal
results.author: Abhishek Prakash
results.content:
Got a headless Raspberry Pi and want to connect to it? You don't need to use your computer for that. You can do that with your smartphone itself.
TechxArtisan's latest gadget turns your smartphone into a keyboard, mouse, gamepad and even a SSH terminal.
These folks gave us KVM-over-USB gadgets like Openterface Mini-KVM and Openterface KVM-GO in the past.
Now they are working on Openterface KeyMod, a tiny USB-bridge that can do a number of things by interacting with a computer from your phone.
Key Specifications
- Microcontroller: WCH CH32V208 RISC-V MCU
- USB functions: HID keyboard and mouse, plus a USB network bridge (SSH, VNC, file transfer), both active at the same time
- Wireless: BLE 5.3 on both models; KeyMod Plus adds a wired USB option for more bandwidth
- Phone app: KeyCmd, for Android (APK available) and iOS (coming soon)
- Two variants: Mini uses USB-C, Plus uses USB-A
Both variants have the same price tag of $24. The project is being crowdfunded on CrowdSupply.
The interesting thing here is not that the keyboard and mouse part. It's that KeyMod does two USB jobs at the same time. Let me explain.
You plug it into the target machine, and it shows up as a USB composite device: a standard HID keyboard and mouse, and a USB network bridge using the CDC-ECM standard, basically working as a private USB Ethernet link. The target gets a fixed IP at 192.168.11.2, your phone lands on 192.168.11.1. No DHCP, no Wi-Fi hunting, no driver to install on most systems.
Because HID input works without an OS loaded, KeyMod reaches BIOS screens, boot menus, and recovery environments too. It is similar to what Openterface Mini-KVM covers, just without the video feed.
On the phone side, the KeyCmd app decides what KeyMod does next. Their description mentions that KM Basic gives you a wireless keyboard, touchpad, and numpad. KM Pro adds a Shortcut Hub and Compose & Send, which lets you draft a long command, API key, or license key on your phone, review it, then fire it off as real keystrokes.
There's also Macros for scripted key sequences, a Presentation mode for Keynote and Google Slides, a Gamepad mode for emulators, and Shortcut Hub profiles for Blender, VS Code, etc.
Do note that KeyCmd is available only in APK format. It is not in Google Play Store. The iOS version has a 'coming soon' tag. I hope this thing is handled before the device gets shipped because Google plans to restrict sideloading of apps and Apple is notorious for raising fence to protect their walled garden.
Now, the network bridge is what makes Terminal (SSH) over BLE or USB possible, without needing a network setup. It works with macOS and Linux targets today. Windows support needs RNDIS instead of CDC-ECM, and that's still in development. Ah! That's so satisfactory as a Linux user ;)
Mini vs Plus
Mini and Plus run the same software, just connected differently.
KeyMod Mini is USB-C, BLE-only, and tiny enough for a keychain or phone lanyard at 25 x 15 x 5 mm and about 2.4 g.
KeyMod Plus is USB-A, adds a wired USB link to the phone for up to 10 Mbps (versus BLE's 2 Mbps), and is built more for staying plugged into servers, legacy PCs, or rack gear.
At $42, it lands close to InputStick ($34) and DexoPad ($39), but neither of those does SSH over BLE the way KeyMod does.
AI Agent Mode
Not only software, it seems like every hardware got to have AI these days.
So, there's also an experimental AI Agent Mode. You add your own LLM API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama whatever you use), describe a goal in plain language like "check logs" or "restart service," and the model plans a sequence of terminal commands, presenting each one for your approval before it runs.
On newer iPhones (14 Pro and up), KeyCmd can also run a small local model instead, TechxArtisan says it has tested a 0.6B Qwen model under 1GB of RAM. It's clearly early, and TechxArtisan itself frames it as likely to stay experimental for a while.
Watch out for...
A couple of things you should know.
BLE encryption isn't turned on yet. The security design is finalized (Bluetooth LE Secure Connections, AES-128, ECDH P-256), but current beta and engineering kits ship without it enabled, with the actual switch-on coming through a firmware update before shipping.
If wireless exposure is a concern for your use case, KeyMod Plus's wired USB link bypasses BLE entirely during operation. CE and UKCA certification are also still in progress, though the company says both are committed before shipping.
On the open source side, KeyCmd for Android and iOS is in development for now and is slated to go fully open source on GitHub once the campaign wraps.
Hardware schematics and PCB files will be published as the project evolves, and OSHWA certification is planned, following Mini-KVM (CN000015) and KVM-GO (CN000022).
One more thing to set expectations on: this campaign's units will most likely ship in the current 3D-printed enclosure rather than an injection-molded one, since tooling would add at least two months to the timeline. Which, I think, means that the product may not look as smooth. If you have ever used 3D printed product, you will understand that.
Getting Openterface KeyMod
Openterface KeyMod is live on Crowd Supply. As of this writing it has raised $9,618 of its $15,000 goal (64%) from 149 backers, with funding closing on Oct 1, 2026.
Both the Mini and Plus are priced at $42, plus $8 shipping in the US or $18 worldwide. Orders placed now are estimated to ship Feb 14, 2027.

TechxArtisan has launched the Openterface KeyMod on CrowdSupply, a versatile USB-bridge device that allows users to control computers and manage headless servers directly from their smartphones.

### Key Points
- The device functions as a composite USB keyboard, mouse, and network bridge, enabling SSH access and file transfers without requiring existing Wi-Fi or DHCP configurations.
- It features a WCH CH32V208 RISC-V microcontroller and supports BLE 5.3, with the "Plus" model offering an additional wired USB connection for higher bandwidth.
- The KeyCmd app provides advanced features including macro scripting, gamepad emulation, and an experimental AI agent mode for executing terminal commands via LLMs.
- Hardware is available in two variants, Mini (USB-C) and Plus (USB-A), both priced at $42 with an estimated shipping date of February 14, 2027.
- The project is slated to become fully open source, with plans for OSHWA certification and future firmware updates to enable AES-128 Bluetooth encryption.

### Why it Matters
This tool simplifies remote server management and hardware troubleshooting by eliminating the need for dedicated peripherals or complex network setups. By providing low-level access to BIOS and recovery environments via a smartphone, it offers a portable, efficient solution for IT professionals and Linux enthusiasts.

results.title: Rebecca Katz’s Risky Formula for Winning Elections
results.author: David Freedlander
results.content:
It’s a few hours before polls close in Michigan, and Rebecca Katz is alone in front of the stage at the Majestic Theatre in Midtown Detroit, pacing. Her candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, is scheduled to have his Election Night party here, and over the last week of the race, his campaign has expressed extreme outward confidence. Polls show him likely to win in a blowout against Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat. The expectation is a short night and a victory speech early in the evening.
But Katz looks miserable, hunched over her phone, twitching, texting reporters and campaign staff, trying to keep an even keel as press file into the auditorium. Michigan is one of the last contested primaries of the year, one of the final places for the left wing of the Democratic Party to stake its claim. Control of the Senate next year, as well as greater checks on Donald Trump’s powers, could hang in the balance. And El-Sayed’s numbers are not looking great. Katz knows if things hold and he does not win easily, with a broad coalition, the party’s trust in his ability to win the November general election will be shaken.
The child of Egyptian immigrants, El-Sayed has campaigned for the Senate on his support for Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, and ending military aid to Israel. If elected in November, he has suggested he would not support Senator Chuck Schumer’s bid for Democratic leader of the body. The idea that El-Sayed could win the nomination would have been laughable a few years ago — when he ran for governor in 2018, he lost in the Democratic primary by 22 points.
Schumer and most of the rest of the Democratic Establishment lined up against him, as they have against Katz’s clients throughout her career: Graham Platner, the upstart progressive from Maine who chased a governor out of the Senate race; Jamaal Bowman, a former Bronx principal who defeated a 16-term incumbent congressman; Senator John Fetterman, the Hells Angels look-alike whom elected Democrats disregarded; and even Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who did not receive the endorsement of party leaders until well after he had secured the Democratic nomination.
In all of those cases, Katz’s candidates won, and she provided crucial strategic advice. However, while there have been a lot of victories, there have also been a number of high-profile disasters. Fetterman has become the Democrats’ No. 1 troll, a Fox News regular who has distanced himself from the party. Bowman lost his reelection bid after a series of blunders, which included pulling a fire alarm during a vote in the House of Representatives. Accusations of sexual assault against Platner, which he denies, have put the Democrats’ hopes of taking the Senate in jeopardy.
El-Sayed is running in Michigan, a traditional home of the working-class, lunch-bucket Democrat and a state President Trump has won twice. It is close to mandatory for Democrats to succeed here. In the Majestic Theatre, no one — especially not Katz — needs to be reminded that there is a lot riding on her unorthodox ideas about who can win a big election in a purple Rust Belt state.
Ever since the Platner implosion, Katz has laid out to me her theory of politics, why it is not crazy to bet on El-Sayed — in fact, why it would be wrong to do the opposite and assume an Establishment candidate could win. She has done it over the course of weeks in near-daily phone calls and texts. Between arguments about why her formula would help Democrats win, she would also make a case for why I shouldn’t write an article about her. When we meet in her office in a tower in Downtown Brooklyn overlooking the Manhattan skyline, the pattern continues. I take out my phone and laptop; she says, “I am not sure I am agreeing to this.” And then Katz proceeds to talk for the next three hours. Often, she interrupts herself to ask who else I was talking to and what they were saying; she asks what the story would really be about. “How about the tension in my own soul?” she suggests, half in jest.
But the reason I am talking to Katz is obvious. Fight Agency, the political-consulting firm she co-founded a little over a year and a half ago with veteran ad makers Tommy McDonald and Julian Mulvey — later bringing in, among others, the 27-year-old wunderkind of left-wing politics, Morris Katz (no relation) — seems to have unlocked a secret for unlikely victories in American politics. For the midterms, the agency has orchestrated the campaigns of underdog and outsider candidates who have won key Democratic Party primaries. Fight’s victories have left the Establishment in a funny position. Despite many of them inveighing against her candidates for months, Democrats now need Katz’s theory of the electorate to work to win back Congress.
Some in the Establishment worry it is a foolish bet on novices aligned with an insurgency from the Democratic Socialists of America. Fight’s roster represents the left edge of the possible in American politics. The candidates chosen are in many cases making their first run for political office. Before the campaign, Platner was an oysterman who had served in the military; El-Sayed was a county public-health official; Dan Osborn, another Fight client mounting a second independent candidacy for a Senate seat in Nebraska, was a mechanic. Bob Brooks, a Fight client hoping to flip a congressional seat in Pennsylvania, was head of a firefighters union. In her work, Katz is explicitly looking for normal people who come from normal backgrounds, not carefully groomed career politicians. “The era of the perfect candidate is over,” she says, repeating a line she often uses when pitching her work. “You’re not looking for a candidate with perfect hair and a perfect life.”
The idea is a direct challenge to strategic orthodoxy in American politics. The way running a campaign is usually understood is that you need to convince some portion of the people who voted for the other party last time to vote for you this time. It’s why Democratic leaders have been optimistic heading into the midterms; as the president’s approval rating sags, Democrats just need some regretful Trump voters to flip. So party leadership has tried to recruit candidates who reassure persuadable Republicans — candidates who aren’t too woke, too left, too radical. Candidates who make people feel they can safely vote for a Democrat and it won’t mean prisons will be abolished, borders eliminated, or the internal-combustion engine outlawed.
Fight’s operating theory is sometimes described as the belief that the true path to victory lies in left-wing populism. But the fact that these candidates are all on the left is, Katz tells me, not her focus. She is far from a wild-eyed socialist or a fire-breathing revolutionary, despite having spent almost a decade and a half pulling the party in a more progressive direction. Katz says her choices are instead based on a belief that Democrats keep getting in their own way by nominating milquetoast candidates who play in the familiar battle lines of partisan politics.
“It’s harder to get candidates who are more in touch with their communities out of primaries,” Katz told Campaigns & Elections, a magazine that covers the political-consulting industry. But “those candidates are out there. They might just not have people who take a serious look at them.” Katz’s unique skill is finding and presenting these candidates to the public. “This is Rebecca’s superpower,” says one rival political operative. “Her ability to brand candidates and create a story around them and a protective marketing bubble and myth and mythology is unmatched.”
Katz’s critics view this “superpower” differently. They say Fight is undermining the work of national Democrats and local parties. “I am not saying these people aren’t smart, but they are playing this political game backward. It is the candidate’s job to find the consultant and not the consultant’s job to find the candidate,” says Jim Kessler, the executive vice-president of policy at Third Way, which supports moderates in the Democratic Party. “You take someone like Platner, and here is this person who looks like he is lifted from central casting, who is handsome and charismatic and articulate, who seems unafraid and who farms oysters, and to the consultants who pluck him out, he is perfect. But it’s just a con.”
Katz thinks such D.C.-brained complaints miss what is actually happening out in the electorate. “The leaders of our party don’t recognize their own toxicity and that there are many different stories to be told and many different kinds of candidates,” she says in her office. “I bet you that Chuck Schumer thinks that Zohran Mamdani is more toxic to the Democratic brand than he is. That is the problem.”
The stereotype of a top political operative is a hard-drinking, fast-living man with mercenary instincts and expensive habits. Katz is the opposite. She is a ball of New York neurosis and chaotic energy whose self-appointed task is saving the Democratic Party from itself. With her, there is no sipping of bourbon or talking about shadowy deals. She is a Brooklyn parent, and when we talk, it is easy to pick up the sounds of her making dinner or shuffling her two teenage boys out the door.
Katz’s first major job on the Hill was with Harry Reid Jr., the pugnacious but soft-spoken majority leader of the Senate. She had grown up in Philadelphia, the child of a social worker and a professor, one of the few white kids in her kindergarten class, and graduated from Central High School, among the city’s elite public high schools. Before her time with Reid, she had worked a job with John Edwards’s presidential campaign, then ran communications in the Pennsylvania operation for an outside spending effort trying to elect John Kerry president.
After the Republicans’ success in Swift-boating Kerry, Reid was determined to find a way for Democrats to go on offense. He acted on Hillary Clinton’s suggestion to create a “war room,” a centralized hub that could push back on Republicans’ attacks. The person he originally hired, Katz says, abruptly quit just before his start date. Katz — broke and directionless after Kerry’s loss — got the job instead.
Reid was a mentor and surprisingly understanding as a boss. Katz is dyslexic and suffers from an undiagnosed attention deficit disorder. One day, she was sitting by Reid with a list of phone numbers from Nevada radio stations he was supposed to call for a series of brief interviews. Katz kept telling him the wrong phone numbers until Reid finally asked, “Do you have a learning disability?” She nodded “yes,” afraid she would be fired. Instead, Reid responded, barely above a whisper, “Well, you must have had to work twice as hard to get where you are.”
“I loved him forever after that,” Katz says.
While her disabilities made working through a call sheet harder, an inability to focus on any one thing for very long has served Katz well as a campaign consultant. She doesn’t read The New Yorker. The Sunday Times arrives with a thump to her doorstep but goes untouched. Books on politics, even ones where she is mentioned, are unopened, and podcasts are too long and boring. Instead, Katz gets her news the way she thinks most voters do, scanning X and TikTok all day, figuring anything worth seeing will show up in her feed.
“She has an acute sense of where the news cycle is at any given moment,” says Lauren Hitt, a former spokesperson for Kamala Harris’s presidential campaign who has worked on several races alongside Katz. “It is very much driven by an idea that it is a waste of time to walk into the day with the same plan you had yesterday. She is comfortable in chaos.”
The close attention to vibes online helps Katz figure out the trajectory of campaigns quickly. In the most recent California gubernatorial primary, she was working for Tom Steyer, the billionaire former hedge-funder, a client who led some of Katz’s detractors in the political-consulting business to claim hypocrisy; Katz told me Steyer convinced her he was the most progressive candidate in the race. After Eric Swalwell dropped out, Steyer briefly looked like the front-runner. But Katz saw the eventual Democratic nominee, Xavier Becerra, gaining steam online before polls and conventional wisdom caught up. She got the campaign to focus on him, an operative who worked on the race tells me. Steyer still lost.
The operative says Katz’s advice helped but there were limits to her formula. “Everyone out here thought Steyer was going to win,” another operative tells me. “But you can’t just show up in California and run a Mamdani-style campaign and call yourself a Bernie Sanders kind of billionaire and expect to win. It was style over substance, and people didn’t buy it.” Katz will soon have another shot in California: Fight has been hired to help DSA member Nithya Raman in her upstart campaign for mayor of Los Angeles.
After a couple of years working for Reid, Katz began to tire of life among Democratic senators. It was a job that consisted mostly of men jostling for attention. She made her way to New York and moved in with her fiancé (now husband), James Katz, whom she’d met on the Edwards campaign. Soon after, she started working with Bill de Blasio, who eventually put together a run for City Hall.
The de Blasio approach set the template for future Katz campaigns: He announced weeks before everyone and ran as an unapologetic progressive. Katz candidates are now known for entering before others, catching the supposed front-runners by surprise, and moving with aggression. The seminal moment of that campaign, Katz says, is when de Blasio spoke at the Association for a Better New York breakfast and told attendees, including some of the city’s elite, that he would raise taxes on the wealthy to help pay for universal pre-K.
But Katz quickly grew disillusioned with de Blasio’s imperiousness, serving only 15 months in his administration. In 2015, she traveled to Braddock, Pennsylvania. A struggling town trying to refashion itself as a haven for artists priced out of New York, Braddock had a six-foot-eight, 300-pound, heavily tattooed mayor who supported Bernie Sanders for president and was contemplating a run for the U.S. Senate. The party was lined up behind Katie McGinty, a former environmental regulator turned lobbyist, to face off against Republican incumbent Pat Toomey in the 2016 general election. But Fetterman seemed to be able to generate real enthusiasm. There were standing-room crowds and hundreds of thousands in small-dollar donations. Katz took him on.
It was hard to convince others to see Fetterman’s potential. Katz accompanied him to Washington, D.C., where officials from the Democratic-campaign Establishment made clear how little they thought of the mayor. “‘We hear you want to legalize heroin,’ they said, and he said, ‘No, you know, I just think that we have a drug crisis in America. I see it in my community, and I think we have to rethink drug policy,’” Katz recalls.
As the race went on, the Democratic Party rallied behind McGinty, including the sitting governor. Former president Barack Obama cut a radio ad for her. Even Sanders didn’t support Fetterman. But Katz, who had a growing rolodex of national political reporters, made her candidate into a brand by steering the media to Braddock to get a look at Fetterman. She framed him as an outsider antidote to the problems of politics.
Fetterman was a graduate of Harvard’s John F. Kennedy School of Government, the son of a successful businessman, and supported by his family well into adulthood. But few of those facts made it into the stories beyond a passing mention. Fetterman was instantly recognizable as something more in line with the needs of the media: a man of forgotten America with a lefty’s heart of gold.
In the 2016 Senate primary, Fetterman would come in a distant third place, but he had established himself in the national consciousness. Six months later, McGinty would lose the general election to Toomey, helping the GOP keep a narrow majority in the Senate.
After Fetterman fizzled out, Katz found herself back in New York, adrift. Trump was president, and, as she saw it, Democrats were too quickly moving on from what happened in 2016, too ready to believe Trump was a fluke. “Democrats lost their way when they stopped being curious about what voters were saying,” she tells me. “They asked no questions about why Hillary Clinton lost. There was no audit, nobody questioning if that playbook was the correct playbook. And if we had just taken a beat to look at the war within the party, to look at why people were excited by Bernie in the first place, and figure out where those Bernie voters went in ’20 and ’24, I think we’d all be better off.”
Young voters, radicalized by Trump’s presidency, were joining the Democratic Socialists of America and forming groups like Justice Democrats, Run for Something, and Sunrise Movement, all of which tried to pull the Democratic Party to the left. Katz was more than a decade older than the senior leadership of these groups but became a mentor to young political operatives, showing them how to deal with the press and how to drive narratives.
“It was like, ‘Oh, you just call these people and paint a story and make it easier for them to write?’” recalls one person who worked with her then. “None of us had any rolodex or relationships, and she came in with this sense that you needed conflict to drive a story further.”
In 2018, Katz became a primary strategist behind the actor Cynthia Nixon’s quixotic run for governor against Andrew Cuomo. The campaign is mostly remembered for how Katz turned something that would typically be hashed in closed-door negotiations — the room temperature for their debate — into a national story that spawned think pieces. (“Can a Room Temperature Be Sexist?” read one headline.) “Ninety percent of the reason I ran was that nobody else would run because everybody was so scared of Cuomo,” Nixon tells me. “And it was very hard to get people, particularly people of her caliber, to work on the campaign because everybody was running scared — and she wasn’t even scared a little bit.”
Katz did worry about her business prospects after taking on the notoriously vindictive Cuomo. But she was also growing more distant from the Establishment and could not hide her frustration. In 2019, the national Democratic Party’s congressional-campaign arm announced that any consulting firm that worked with someone challenging an incumbent would be blacklisted. “I just wanted them to be curious about what works in politics and where all this energy was coming from,” she says of party leaders. “And they just wanted to end my career.”
In 2022, Fetterman again ran for the Senate, and the party Establishment, believing him to be a weak general-election candidate, again supported a rival. This time it was Representative Conor Lamb, who, with his square jaw, earnest mien, and military background, looked like the perfect fit to defeat the Republican candidate, the TV personality Mehmet Oz.
But something had shifted between 2016 and 2022. Maybe the party Establishment didn’t have the power it once did. Or maybe Democratic-primary voters had caught up to what Katz had been pushing the previous six years. Fetterman won by more than 20 points.
“My model for that race was really the Obama campaign,” Katz says. “Everybody keeps learning the lessons of Bill Clinton over and over again, but they think it’s about triangulation when it’s really two things: ‘It’s the economy, stupid’ and ‘I feel your pain.’ It was Obama who really showed us how to run a populist campaign, criticizing Mitt Romney for how many houses he has. It’s the kind of thing that’s sticky.”
Fetterman won by five points, despite running in a general election that was supposed to be a difficult environment for Democrats and, more importantly, despite the fact that he had a stroke right before the primary and struggled to speak for much of the race.
Katz was thrilled. She and Fetterman had been friends for nearly a decade, and this was proof her way of doing politics could succeed in a swing state — that Democrats could run nontraditional, pathbreaking candidates who popped on social media and connected with voters in ways the stuffy mainstream could not. Fetterman’s candidacy didn’t doom Democrats, Katz believed; it saved them from almost certain defeat. After the win, Katz bought her own ticket to a fundraiser for Bob Casey, the other Pennsylvania Democratic senator, who was gearing up for his own challenging reelection campaign. There, she buttonholed him on the work she and some of her colleagues had done for Fetterman and tried to pitch him on the same approach.
“I said, ‘This is going to be a hard race, and I think you need to punch him in the fucking face,’” Katz recalls. The genteel Casey, the scion of a Pennsylvania Democratic dynasty, demurred. “And he was like, ‘Oh, that’s so kind of you.’ He was so polite. And I said we could put together, like, a team and we could go hard. Like, ‘I think you have to go hard against the Republicans.’” Casey declined. He went on to lose.
Instead of another job in Pennsylvania, Katz went to work for Ruben Gallego, a progressive Arizona congressman who was raised by a single mom before deploying to Iraq and eventually making his way to Harvard University. Gallego talked like a regular person, encouraging Democrats to stop using terms like “economic stability” and instead recognize that most voters, especially men, just wanted a job, a place of their own, and “a big-ass truck.” Gallego followed the Katz playbook: He announced early, blitzed the state, and chased the recently independent sitting senator, Kyrsten Sinema, out of the race. He won in 2024 and outperformed Kamala Harris in the state.
Afterward, Katz and some veterans of the Fetterman campaign decided to start their own agency. ARE YOU A FIGHT CANDIDATE? read a rubric the group created when it was first forming. “Can you have a conversation that doesn’t sound like talking points?,” one prompt read. “Can you tell me why you are running for office in one sentence? Do you have a connection to the working class?” If you answered “yes,” then you were ready for Fight. If you answered “yes” to the question “Were you voted most likely to be president in your high-school yearbook?,” Fight would hustle you out the door.
“The idea was to go on offense. We wanted people who weren’t scared of their own shadow all the time,” says Kipp Hebert, a longtime associate of Katz’s. “One thing we always say is that Democrats should stop apologizing for being Democrats. The Republicans are confident in who they are, and their party leaders don’t spend all their time talking about how some of their candidates are liabilities.”
As much as Fight has been painted as the political-consulting firm of the rising left, that is not quite right. Fight is not associated with the DSA, and the agency did not help every candidate associated with the organization this cycle. Katz’s firm, for instance, did not work with Francesca Hong, the legislator and chef who lost a gubernatorial primary in Wisconsin.
Fight’s idea is not to support so-called regular people — regular people don’t run for office; it is to support real people, those who have personality and are confident in who they are. Conventional wisdom in Washington has maintained that the key to Trump’s rise was his willingness to moderate and break from Republican orthodoxy on issues like Medicare and Social Security; Katz and the team at Fight don’t buy it. Trump wins because, as Hebert puts it, “he talks about the elite that you hate while Democrats talk about how we are going to make your life incrementally better in a way that you won’t even notice. Trump is saying ‘Let’s tear the system down,’ and Democrats are saying ‘Let’s make the system better with 100 small ideas’ but not paint a picture of a better future.”
The primaries haven’t always borne out the idea that the Democrats are simply too cautious. In Michigan, the result was far closer than the polls had it. The race was not called, as expected, that night. It took until early the following morning, long after the Majestic had emptied for the evening. El-Sayed eked out a victory by a single percentage point. If those moderate Democrats who voted against El-Sayed in the primary prove unwilling to support him in the general against the relatively centrist Republican Mike Rogers, the race will be hard to win.
And for all the talk of working-class politics, El-Sayed actually did far worse among those voters than Stevens. Likewise, Platner was performing poorly among working-class voters in Maine when he dropped out. “Fight folks have this idea that poor people are closet leftists, and they are just not,” says a former top Democratic official. “The people who come out for them are college-educated people who like the videos they see on social media.”
When Fight began in early 2025, it seemed to have a growing track record in statewide races. It had already helped elect two straight-talking lawmakers from swing states in Fetterman and Gallego. But Bowman had imploded and Fetterman had broken ties with the progressive wing, and in a few months’ time, Morris Katz was traveling to Maine to recruit Platner for his doomed run. It began to look like a pattern: Fight could pick people to win elections in the Trump era — the problem was what happens next.
Rebecca Katz, ever the comms pro, doesn’t much want to talk about what has gone wrong with some of her candidates. She thinks October 7 had something to do with it in two cases — it pushed Fetterman right and Bowman further left while also making the latter less responsive to the concerns of his constituents. “I do think there’s something about the way that campaigns are today,” Katz says. “They are all-encompassing and suffocating, and it comes at you from every angle. And they don’t just go after you; they go after the people you love. And I think it does alter the brain chemistry a little bit.”
The Fetterman case is clearly a wound. She considered him a friend, enjoyed his company, and spent a decade trying to get him to the U.S. Senate. Then he got there and became a different person. In her view, the darkness he had kept at bay seemed to have overtaken him. It nags at her. What if Fetterman switches parties after Democrats take the chamber? Worse, what if he does only after El-Sayed wins just as a way to get back at Katz?
Platner is different. He went through multiple tours in Iraq, and she believes it left a mark. “Fetterman’s life was hard from inside,” she told me. “I think Graham’s life was hard from the outside.” Katz and her team at Fight still stand behind the idea of Platner — at the beginning, he was a good candidate and forced a sitting governor from the race. But, as Katz says, “if he committed sexual assault, he should not be a U.S. senator. It’s as simple as that.”
It’s a dilemma, then, for both Katz and for the Democratic Party. She keeps finding candidates who are exciting to voters. But that formula can lead to blowups and reversals that endanger the broader prospects of the party.
“Our whole theory of the case has been that basically people don’t care if their candidates are broken because they are a little bit broken too,” Katz says as the sun is setting outside her office window. “They don’t care if their candidates are flawed because everyone is flawed, right? You are looking for someone who has been through what you’ve been through and they understand you and they see you. That is the theory.”
“I don’t think I should be responsible for all of my candidates’ worst decisions,” she adds. “I am hired to win races.”

- Several high-profile candidates associated with Katz have faced significant controversies, including Jamaal Bowman’s primary loss and allegations against Graham Platner.

### Why it Matters
Katz’s methodology represents a fundamental shift in how progressive campaigns identify and market candidates to voters in a polarized political climate. While her firm has successfully secured key primary victories, the resulting volatility of these candidates creates ongoing tension regarding the Democratic Party's ability to maintain a cohesive and reliable governing coalition.

results.author: staff@bgr.com (Joshua Hawkins)
results.content:
Amazon Devices Just Got A Lot More Expensive Thanks To The Memory Crisis
If you look at Amazon this week, you might notice that much of Amazon's hardware has become noticeably more expensive. The company quietly raised its prices across the board, including on devices like its Echo, Kindle, Fire TV, and eero lineups. While not every price hike is huge, there are some pretty substantial increases.
The Echo Dot has now jumped from $49.99 to $79.99 while Amazon's 16GB Kindle rose from $109.99 to $149.99. The 16GB Kindle Paperwhite increased from $159.99 to $199.99, too, and even the Fire TV Stick 4K Max has seen a hike, rising to $84.99 instead of its previous $59.99. Ring products weren't included in the increases at this time, however, but a number of the company's eero devices saw price hikes as well.
Amazon says rising component costs are the big bad to blame, with the company telling Fortune that the consumer electronics industry is dealing with "significant increases in memory and storage component costs." Much like the other companies that have followed this pattern in the past several months, Amazon claims that it had absorbed those costs for as long as it could before raising its prices.
Amazon isn't alone
Amazon might be the latest to raise hardware prices, but it has plenty of company. Roku raised prices on its streaming devices in July, with the company also blaming the rising memory prices as the primary driver. With Roku, these changes pose questions about the company's future as an affordable streaming platform, but Amazon doesn't face the same scrutiny. That's because its biggest devices — like Kindles — face some competition, but are largely in a powerful position in their respective market.
Other big tech companies such as Apple also raised prices, with the Mac, iPad, Apple TV, HomePod, and several other products getting a hike back in June. The base iPad went from $349 to $449, while the MacBook Neo increased from $599 to $699. The iPhone didn't see a price increase this time around, but it's likely only a matter of time until it does.
Samsung raised prices on a number of Galaxy phones, tablets, and laptops too. On phones, the increases mostly hit higher-storage configurations, with several 512GB and 1TB models going up by $80. Tablets were hit much harder, though, with the 512GB Galaxy Tab S11 climbing from $979.99 to $1,199.99. Meanwhile, the 1TB Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra jumped from $1,619.99 to $1,899.99. Samsung's laptops weren't spared either, with the 1TB Galaxy Book 6 Ultra increasing by $450, from $2,449.99 to $2,899.99.
Memory isn't getting cheaper, yet
Unfortunately, the price hikes are unlikely to stop there, either. TrendForce currently expects DRAM prices to jump another 13% to 18% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 2026, while NAND Flash prices are expected to climb between 10% to 15% higher than their current listings. As those prices increase on the manufacturer side, TrendForce expects that will trickle down to consumers even more, especially when looking at more expensive devices like laptops. In fact, we've already seen some companies discussing returning to 8GB of RAM as the standard for newer laptops in 2026 and onward.
The core of the problem, of course, is still AI. As data centers continue to expand and memory manufacturers shift more of their capacity toward creating server-based DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, the room for consumer-grace PC components is shrinking. And those areas of AI-focused manufacturing are expected to grow nearly 31% year over year in the most recent forecasts.
Adding more supply isn't something manufacturers can do overnight, either. Samsung, SK Hynix and other suppliers are already expanding production, but this takes time to build and ramp up. New DRAM capacity isn't expected to really make a meaningful difference until the second half of 2027, or the following year, while it's possible NAND could get relief sooner.
results.summary:
Amazon has quietly increased prices across its Echo, Kindle, Fire TV, and eero hardware lineups, citing significant rising costs for memory and storage components within the electronics industry.

### Key Points
- The Echo Dot price increased from $49.99 to $79.99, while the 16GB Kindle rose from $109.99 to $149.99.
- Amazon attributed the hikes to industry-wide surges in memory and storage component costs that the company can no longer absorb.
- Other major tech firms, including Roku, Apple, and Samsung, have recently implemented similar price increases across their respective hardware portfolios.
- Market analysts at TrendForce project DRAM prices will rise another 13% to 18% in Q3 2026, further pressuring consumer electronics pricing.
- High demand for AI-focused server memory is limiting supply for consumer devices, with significant production relief not expected until late 2027 or 2028.

### Why it Matters
These widespread price hikes signal a sustained period of inflation for consumer electronics as manufacturers prioritize high-bandwidth memory for AI data centers. Consumers should expect continued cost increases and potential hardware downgrades, such as reduced RAM standards, until global production capacity catches up to demand.
